YOGA-2019DEC-P2-Q141.question_text: With reference to the above passage, name the practical philosophy:

YOGA-2019DEC-P2-Q143.passage:
Yoga is a system of practical philosophy followed since ancient times. Yoga philosophy developed through the Samkhya shastra. 'Samkhya' means number; in the Samkhya shastra, as awareness grows, a person becomes able to enumerate things from the outer to the inner, and groups and classifies them for experience.

The application of knowledge creates prosperity (aishvarya) and accomplishment (vibhuti). Supreme knowledge gives rise to practical knowledge, and that brings prosperity. So if a person knows the order of the tattvas and their relationships, he gains the power to refine those tattvas with respect to his body, mind and self, and the world beyond.

Yoga rests entirely on the Samkhya philosophy, with supreme importance given to Ishvara. Yoga recognises 26 tattvas. In yoga practice, the integration of these tattvas, which is attained through experience, matters more. All dietary habits, lifestyle and all yogic practices are meant to achieve this goal.

So, for the harmony of the 'tattva traya' of body, mind and self, dietary habits, lifestyle and other factors should support the yogic practices. A wise person adopts these practices in life and attains better health from the physical level to the mental level and to ever higher levels.

The five organs of action and the five organs of knowledge are closely interrelated, since both arise from buddhi. So refining and transforming buddhi affects our organs of knowledge and of action. Therefore direct and indirect mental concentration, that is, meditation and asana, should also influence the organs of knowledge, the organs of action and the five great elements that are inherent in us.

The foods we choose and receive are all decided by the mind. In the same way, assimilation and nourishment are also governed by buddhi, and so any condition that creates a favourable environment for pollutants, or any malfunction, is also related to buddhi. In short, yoga therapy is simply the application of practices according to a person's yogic need. The Bhagavad Gita rightly says "uddhared ātmanātmānam" (one should lift oneself by oneself), and this applies to yoga therapy.

On this basis, yoga therapy can be developed by giving more importance to the 'triguna'. Likewise, Ayurveda, an allied branch of Indian learning, has been developed with emphasis on the 'tridosha'.

YOGA-2019DEC-P2-Q147.question_text: What is verbal knowledge without a real object called?
YOGA-2019DEC-P2-Q147.passage: Yoga is defined as the restraint of the modifications (vrittis) of the chitta. The chitta is made up of three factors: manas (mind), buddhi (intellect) and ahamkara (ego). The chitta is the vehicle of observation, attention, aim and reasoning. The vrittis of the chitta are classified into five classes, and each may be klishta (painful) or aklishta (not painful). They are: pramana (the source of right knowledge), viparyaya (false knowledge), vikalpa (imagination), nidra (sleep) and smriti (memory). Pramana is of three kinds: pratyaksha (direct evidence), anumana (inference) and agama (scriptural evidence); right or correct knowledge can be obtained from these three sources. Viparyaya arises from wrong or illusory knowledge, which mistakes one thing for another and is not based on reality. Vikalpa is mere verbal knowledge without any real object. Nidra is dreamless sleep in which all activity of thought and feeling ceases. Smriti is the unmodified recollection of words and experiences. Practising abhyasa (repeated practice) together with vairagya (dispassion) is the right way to control these five restless states of the chitta. Steady practice of yoga establishes balance in body, mind and self, and calms the restlessness of the chitta, so that it cannot distort the true expression of the self in any way. Only then does the self rest in its own nature, for the attainment of kaivalya.
